## The Coast's Thermometer: Motril, 300 Days of Sun

The Motril weather station, managed by the Agencia Estatal de Meteorología, records a figure that defines the character of this coastal strip: a historical average of 320 clear days a year. Average rainfall barely reaches 300 millimeters annually, an amount that in the neighboring Sierra Nevada is exceeded in a single winter month. This water imbalance, far from being a limitation, has shaped an agricultural ecosystem that exists nowhere else on the Iberian Peninsula.

Winter temperatures rarely drop below 10 degrees Celsius, even during the early hours of January. This thermal threshold acts as an invisible shield that protects crops impossible to grow in inland Granada, where frosts are frequent from November onwards. The tropical coast, the name given to this shoreline, owes its name precisely to that stability which allows the development of subtropical species in the heart of continental Europe.

Cherry tomato and avocado greenhouses stretch out like a sea of white plastic between the A-7 highway and the first foothills of the mountain range. The "El Sol" Agricultural Cooperative, which brings together more than 400 farmers in the area, has documented an average advance of three weeks in harvests over the last decade. Cooperative technicians attribute this phenomenon to the sustained increase in minimum nighttime temperatures, which have risen by 1.2 degrees since 2015, according to the annual records from the Motril station.

The Motril microclimate functions as a natural greenhouse that amplifies the efficiency of artificial structures. While in Almería farmers rely almost exclusively on plastic to retain heat, in Motril the proximity of the Mediterranean acts as a thermal regulator that reduces energy consumption. Sea breezes, laden with relative humidity, penetrate through the Guadalfeo valley and soften the peak summer heat that plagues other Andalusian coastal areas.

Records from the Motril station show a surprisingly low daily thermal oscillation for such a southern latitude. The difference between the maximum and minimum temperatures rarely exceeds 8 degrees, a figure that contrasts with the 20-degree oscillation recorded in the Granada plateau. This stability reduces physiological stress on the plants and allows harvests to be scheduled with almost industrial precision.

Rainfall, concentrated in just 25 days a year, necessitates meticulous water management. The cooperative's farmers have developed drip irrigation systems that take advantage of the Sierra Nevada snowmelt, channeled through the centuries-old irrigation ditches that descend through the ravines. The water that irrigates the Motril avocados originates at 3,000 meters above sea level and takes less than 48 hours to reach the roots of the trees.

AEMET data confirm that Motril records more annual sunshine hours than any other point in the province of Granada. The 3,200 hours of direct sunlight received by this coastline even surpass iconic Andalusian tourism areas such as Marbella or Cádiz. This constant radiation accelerates ripening cycles and concentrates sugars in the fruits, a factor that European buyers particularly value in cherry tomatoes.

The "El Sol" Agricultural Cooperative has installed temperature and humidity sensors on a dozen pilot farms to monitor microclimatic conditions in real time. Data collected over the last five campaigns reveal that plots located less than 500 meters from the coastline maintain nighttime temperatures up to 3 degrees higher than those located 3 kilometers inland. This thermal gradation allows for staggered planting and the distribution of supply throughout the year.

The poniente wind, which descends dry and warm from the peaks of Sierra Nevada, plays an ambivalent role in this climatic balance. During winter, these gusts can raise temperatures to 20 degrees in a matter of hours, a phenomenon local farmers know as "el terral". However, when it blows with a force exceeding 40 kilometers per hour, it forces the closing of greenhouse vents and can damage avocado flowers during full pollination.

The salinity of the air, another distinctive factor of this coastline, impregnates the crops with a nuance that organoleptic analyses detect in blind tastings. Cooperative technicians have found that tomatoes grown less than a kilometer from the sea present slightly higher sodium levels, a characteristic that gourmet markets in Northern Europe are beginning to value as a mark of origin.

The three-week advance in harvests documented by the cooperative has direct economic consequences. Motril's cherry tomatoes reach Central European markets when Moroccan production has not yet peaked and prices remain high. This window of opportunity, which has progressively widened since 2015, allows local farmers to obtain margins that compensate for the high production costs of a labor-intensive crop.

The Motril weather station, located next to the fishing port, holds historical records dating back to 1950. Analysis of these records reveals that the average annual temperature has risen by 1.8 degrees over the last 75 years, an increase higher than the global average. Winters have shortened and summers have lengthened, a trend that farmers perceive as a short-term opportunity but that climatologists view with caution.

Water availability, rather than temperature, is emerging as the limiting factor for the future of this agricultural model. The reservoirs that regulate the flow of the Guadalfeo depend on snowfall in Sierra Nevada, a resource that climate models project to be in decline. The cooperative has begun experimenting with avocado varieties more resistant to drought and with controlled deficit irrigation patterns that reduce consumption without penalizing production.

The Motril microclimate is not a static phenomenon but a dynamic system that responds to the interaction between the Mediterranean, the mountains, and the atmosphere. The average of 320 days of sun recorded by the weather station is the most visible manifestation of a balance that sustains an agricultural economy valued at over 200 million euros annually. The next time a cherry tomato from the tropical coast arrives at a supermarket in Berlin or Stockholm, it will carry with it the thermal signature of this corner of southern Granada.
